text: Curricular Practical Training (CPT) Protocol Effective May 6, 2021 | International Student and Scholar Services | University of Colorado Boulder Skip to main content Search Enter the terms you wish to search for. This site All of Colorado.edu Other ways to search: Events Calendar Campus Map Advising Services MyISSS Portal Departmental Services Immigration Alerts & FAQs Curricular Practical Training (CPT) Protocol Effective May 6, 2021 Published:2/1/2021 2/1/2021 Curricular Practical Training (CPT) is a temporary training authorization for an “alternative work/study, internship, cooperative education, or any other type of required internship or practicum which is offered by sponsoring employers through cooperative agreements with the school.” ISSS is updating our Curricular Practical Training (CPT) protocol to ensure that CU Boulder maintains compliance with the Department of Homeland Security F-1 visa regulations and is more closely aligned with the CPT policies of our peer institutions. CPT must be an integral part of your major curriculum, supported by either a credit bearing internship class or required for your major for any CPT authorized for May 6, 2021 or later. You must meet one of the following requirements for CPT, which your major department must sign off on: Be enrolled in an internship course for credit that counts towards your degree. (Enrollment in the course must be concurrent with the training. For example, if the internship is in the summer, you must be enrolled in the internship course during the summer) or Your degree must require an internship and that requirement is clearly documented in the University Catalog . If you do not meet the requirements for the CPT protocol effective May 6, 2021, then you have the option to apply for pre-completion OPT for off-campus work authorization. Please review ISSS’s Pre-completion OPT webpage and ISSS Pre-Completion OPT Guide for information on pre-completion OPT. ISSS understands the impact this change in CPT protocol may have on our international students in F-1 status who would like to take advantage of off-campus training opportunities. However, this change is necessary in order to ensure both CU Boulder and our international students in F-1 status are in compliance with federal rules. text: Groups Tied to Harvard Sue DHS Over New Limits on International Student Internships | The Harvard Crimson The Harvard Crimson Advertisement Advertisement News Groups Tied to Harvard Sue DHS Over New Limits on International Student Internships A coalition of higher education groups with ties to Harvard sued the Department of Homeland Security Monday over new restrictions on Curricular Practical Training for international students. | By E. Matteo Diaz By Sebastian B. Connolly and Summer E. Rose , Crimson Staff Writers A coalition of higher education groups sued the Department of Homeland Security Monday, alleging that two August directives restricting which internships international students can take part in on student visas had caused “irreparable harm” to students and institutions. In a 44-page filing in federal court in Massachusetts, lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that the DHS had engaged in “procedurally invalid” rulemaking reinterpreting the rules governing Curricular Practical Training — a program allowing international students to participate in internships and experiential learning opportunities — to allow it only for internships that every student in a degree program must complete to graduate. The Student and Exchange Visitor Program, which certifies schools to enroll international students, detailed the interpretation of the rule in two broadcast messages on Aug. 12 and 24. In the messages, SEVP officials framed the update as a reminder of existing policy — and warned that universities could lose their SEVP certification, which would bar them from hosting students on visas. The Aug. 12 message also warned that improper authorizations could expose individual school officials, not just their institutions, to “administrative or legal consequences.” In Monday’s suit, lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that the broadcasts are “impermissibly retroactive,” exposing those officials to “criminal prosecution” for past conduct that complied with the government’s position at the time. But in Monday’s filing, lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that the messages broke with more than 35 years of precedent in how the rule had been interpreted — and were an attempt to introduce new legislative rules without abiding by federal procedure governing administrative action. Harvard has ties to all four plaintiffs in the Monday suit: the Association of American Universities, Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA: Association of International Educators, and the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts. The University is a member of AAU, AICUM, and the Presidents’ Alliance, and staff in the Harvard International Office are NAFSA members. Harvard is among several universities to have halted CPT authorizations following the August messages. Five of its schools — Harvard College, Harvard Law School, Harvard Medical School, the Graduate School of Design, and the Graduate School of Arts and Sciences — no longer authorize CPT, and the HIO updated its website to reflect the new guidance. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology, University of Pennsylvania, and Wellesley College are among the schools that have paused authorization of CPT applications since the messages were issued. Get The Crimson in your inbox. Sign up The complaint asks a judge to “restore” the previous interpretation, which allowed students to use CPT for internships taken for academic credit, arguing that the change had already harmed students and schools. “Action is needed now,” the lawyers wrote. “Students have already lost critical internship and research opportunities for the current semester and institutions have had to scramble to determine how ongoing practicums, internships extended from last summer, and applications for future internships might be impacted.” In a separate motion filed Monday night, the plaintiffs asked the court to block DHS from enforcing the new interpretation while the case proceeds. A DHS spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment The August messages come after a series of federal moves to tighten restrictions on international students. In July, DHS announced a rule that would place a fixed four-year limit on student visas and restrict students’ ability to switch programs. Three of the plaintiffs in Monday’s complaint — the Presidents’ Alliance, NAFSA, and AICUM — are suing to block the rule. On Sept. 14, a day before the rule was set to take effect, a federal judge temporarily blocked it. The government has since appealed the ruling, and the case is ongoing. Advertisement Harvard is engaged in its own lawsuit over the Trump administration’s attempt in May 2025 to revoke its SEVP certification — a case that plaintiffs cited in their separate Monday memorandum seeking an injunction noting that a federal judge had recognized evidence that losing SEVP certification can “irreparably harm” a university. The judge in that case blocked the revocation with a preliminary injunction in June 2025. text: Higher education leaders file lawsuit against ICE over international student internship restrictions Skip to main content Higher ed leaders sue Trump administration over limitations on international student internships Print this Article View Comments The Moakley Federal Courthouse on Boston Harbor Lane Turner/Globe Staff A coalition of higher education leaders filed a lawsuit Monday in Boston challenging the federal government’s recent interpretation of an internship program for international students, which plaintiffs say will limit student access to work experience and weaken America’s edge in talent recruitment. The lawsuit comes in response to messages US Immigration and Customs Enforcement emailed to university administrators in August that abruptly shifted the requirements for Curricular Practical Training (CPT), a program that allows international students to participate in internships, co-ops, and other temporary work programs related to their studies. The messages declared that students will only be eligible for CPT if the work opportunity is a graduation requirement for all students in a particular degree program, regardless of citizenship. “This action is yet another attempt by the [Trump] administration to dissuade talented international students from continuing their education in America,” Rob McCarron, president of the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, one of the plaintiffs in the case, said in a statement. When contacted by The Boston Globe, an ICE spokesperson said the agency does not comment on pending litigation. According to statistics from ICE , 130,586 foreign students obtained work authorization through CPT in 2024. The top employers of CPT participants in that year included Amazon, Tesla, and Google. Some universities have already limited CPT authorizations ahead of the fall 2026 semester; Harvard University , Massachusetts Institute of Technology , Boston University , Tufts University , and Suffolk University are among the Massachusetts schools that have all temporarily paused most new and pending CPT authorization requests. All five schools are members of AICUM. Several schools in the University of California system, such as the University of California Berkeley , have paused their course-credit work experiences altogether. The Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, another plaintiff in the new case, claimed that some students have already lost work positions they secured months prior as a result of these institutional changes. McCarron, president of the independent colleges group, said the ICE messages have caused “substantial disruptions” on campuses across Massachusetts as schools were forced to abruptly readapt longstanding processes surrounding student work experiences. In the messages sent Aug. 12 and 24, ICE claims that the Student and Exchange Visitor Program has observed a rise in schools issuing CPT authorizations that violate the requirement that work experience to be an “integral part of an established curriculum.” While the text of the regulatory requirements for CPT has not changed, it seems ICE’s interpretation of the word “integral” has shifted. The ICE messages warned that any institution found in violation could be investigated and lose certification to enroll international students. The plaintiffs said the new interpretation of CPT requirements has left long-standing campus practices like co-op programs in limbo without allowing adequate time for schools to respond or take public comment. The lawsuit also alleges that the communications were sent directly to campus university designated school officials — the employees in charge of advising international students and ensuring the university’s compliance with law — and threatened them with institutional penalties and personal liability for allowing previous CPT practices to continue. The lawsuit includes a motion for a preliminary injunction to force the government to stop any changes to CPT immediately, and as long as the case is active. The Presidents’ Alliance and several other plaintiffs in the case previously sued the Department of Homeland Security over limits on how long international students can stay on certain visas; a case that is ongoing. text: What suspended Curricular Practical Training means for international students – The Wellesley News Skip to Content What suspended Curricular Practical Training means for international students Alicia Zhang , Contributing Writer | October 8, 2026 Photo Courtesy of The New York Times A rally for international students at Harvard University On Sept. 28 of this year, a letter from President Paula Johnson to the international students changed the educational trajectory of students at Wellesley College. The letter announced an indefinite pause on Curricular Practical Training (CPT), a temporary work authorization that lets international students on F-1 visas have the opportunity to seek off-campus practical work experience. With CPT no longer being an option, international students will need to rely heavily on the two experiential learning requirement (ELR) credits that allow them to pursue internships and research experiences. In a political environment that becomes increasingly hostile to international students, Wellesley’s ELR requirement carries sobering implications. Effective for students arriving at Wellesley in fall 2024 and beyond, the ELR asks students to complete two units before their senior year, fulfilled by either one summer-long or two semester-long experiences. By including a variety of choices — from internships and on-campus jobs to community service and civic engagement — the ELR encourages students to develop a well-rounded portfolio for future degrees and careers. However, after CPT was paused, if an international student has already fulfilled the two ELR units, any research or internship opportunities are not authorized. This is an issue especially for upperclassmen who have already completed certain fellowships and CareerEd programs that have automatically counted toward their ELR units. What was initially designed to encourage students to engage in various career-preparatory opportunities has now become a tight thing to manage. This abrupt policy change leaves current international students at a disadvantage. Additionally, future students may choose only two research or internship experiences to count toward their two required ELR units, rather than considering other valuable opportunities. The suspension of CPT was driven by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) , a direct program division within the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). SEVP’s increased scrutiny of CPT approvals was justified by the claim that it “has observed a rise in CPT authorizations that do not meet regulatory requirements, specifically those not constituting an integral part of an established curriculum.” From SEVP’s perspective, only those experiences directly required for obtaining a degree count as “ an integral part of an established curriculum ,” which gives the ludicrous implication that any additional learning is unnecessary and — more problematically — prohibited by the U.S. government. The politically charged statements given by SEVP confirm the blatant assault on the international student community: “DSOs [Designated School Officials] are reminded that F nonimmigrant students are, by their own attestation under penalty of perjury, here in the United States ‘solely for the purpose of pursuing a full program of study.’” Universities are also threatened with “additional scrutiny and action from SEVP and Homeland Security Investigations” if “SEVP suspects that school officials are abusing CPT to create work opportunities rather than academic studies.” The long promised opportunity in American higher education is vilified as an abuse of CPT. The distinct separation of “academic studies” from “work opportunities” also reflects the political agenda of limiting opportunities for foreigners to stay in the country. The discontinuation of CPT is not the first attack on international students; it is the culmination of cutthroat policies that have pushed international students into dreadful struggles. Earlier this July, Trump issued a Final Rule to eliminate the long-standing “duration of status” admission for J-1 Exchange Visitors and F-1 students. Although this rule has been blocked by a federal judge, if it were to take effect, it would create significant hassles for international students who need more than four years to complete their enrolled program or degree. Moreover, it demonstrates Trump’s antagonism toward international students and immigrants. This goes hand in hand with the CPT suspens ion and depriving international students of a chance to extend learning beyond their degree. International students make up roughly 14% of Wellesley’s student body; nationwide, 1.2 million international students are affected by current hostile policies. This part of the Wellesley community includes some of the most vulnerable students, yet these students receive less support than they deserve. The College, for example, could make ELR more flexible to help international students seize the academic and career opportunities they urgently need. Giving students the autonomy to choose which experiences count towards the two required units could be one pragmatic solution. Overall, there should be stronger support systems in place to help international students fight back against the consequences of volatile policy shifts. text: The New School restricts CPT work authorization for international students – The New School Free Press Skip to content News Oct 11, 2026 The New School restricts CPT work authorization for international students By: Aidan Cummins The University Center. Photo by Dove Williams The New School has temporarily restricted Curricular Practical Training (CPT) authorization for international students whose employment is not a part of required curriculum, according to an Aug. 28 email from International Student and Scholar Services (ISSS). Under the new restrictions CPT will only be authorized if internships or experiences are required to graduate. CPT, established in 1947, is a form of work authorization that allows eligible international students to participate in work, internships, clinical placement, and other learning environments related to their major and is a fundamental part of curriculums. This comes after a broadcast message named “Reminder of Liability” from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) on Aug. 12. The message tightened restrictions on interpretations of CPT, limiting all universities’ ability to grant F-1 students off-campus employment. “CPT cannot be authorized solely for the purpose of employment or for experiences that are not required or otherwise formally recognized as part of the academic program,” SEVP’s broadcast message said. “Failure to comply with SEVP regulations may result in an institution losing certification to enroll foreign students,” SEVP said in a follow up broadcast message for “guidance” on Aug. 24. “It’s extremely restrictive to basically say every program, if that program doesn’t have a requirement to do a CPT in it to graduate, you can’t be approved,” Jim Deleppo, director of ISSS at The New School said. With over 3,500 international students at The New School, ISSS works with approximately 2,900 full-time F-1 students and around 1,100 students on post-completion work authorizations, according to Deleppo. Currently The New School requires internship credit for some programs at the graduate and PhD level. Specifically, The Arts Management and Entrepreneurship MA and c linical psychology PhD . Deleppo said the federal policy reflects a stricter interpretation of existing CPT regulations rather than a change to the guidelines themselves.“It wasn’t a change in regulation. It was an interpretation of that particular regulation by SEVP … to basically try to outline it and make the policies stricter at universities,” he said. Since the restriction international students are advised to refrain from off-campus employment without authorization. Unauthorized employment could impact immigration status and future immigration benefits, the university said on Aug. 28th. The New School’s Career Services previously described CPT as the most common form of off-campus work authorization for F-1 students during their academic programs. Most recently on Oct. 5, the Association of American Universities (AAU), which is composed of 71 universities, filed a formal lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security, Department of Justice, and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which oversees SEVP. Explanation As an F-1 student, you may only work off campus in the U.S. if you have received special written work authorization approved by the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). The following information will explain one type of USCIS off-campus work authorization that can only be taken BEFORE COMPLETION OF STUDIES called, “curricular practical training,” or “CPT.” USCIS defines “curricular practical training” as employment that is an integral or important part of your curriculum, including: alternate work/study, internship, cooperative education, or any other type of required employment, internship or practicum. To be considered curricular practical training, the work must be related to your major field of study, and must also be an integral or important part of your studies. Training which is REQUIRED by your degree program always meets the requirements for curricular practical training, regardless of whether or not you receive academic credit for your work. If the internship, work or or volunteer opportunity is related to your major field of study, you should still apply for CPT authorization even if you will not receive payment . The definition of "employment" in immigration terms does not necessarily equate with being paid, and Homeland Security expects international students engaged in unpaid internships to be authorized for CPT. This includes students who may be registering for internship credit through their academic department. Training which is NOT REQUIRED by your degree program may meet the requirements for curricular practical training if you receive academic credit for the employment experience. If you have a training opportunity, which involves employment, check with the international student coordinator to determine if it qualifies as CPT. You must have a job to be authorized for this type of practical training. II. Highlights A job offer is REQUIRED to be authorized for CPT. The employment must be an integral or important part of your curriculum, but can occur anywhere in the U.S. Students must be enrolled an official practicum/internship course, or the work must be a requirement for everyone in the degree program. Changing employers is allowed only AFTER receiving additional approval and authorization for the new employer. CPT authorization is granted by the Office of International Student Services (ISS). During the period of CPT, students are in F-1 visa status since CPT is considered to be part of the program of study. III. Conditions and Limitations You must have a specific position that is directly related to your major field of study and it must be appropriate for someone having your level of education. You must have been enrolled as a full-time student in legal non-immigrant status for at least 9 months before CPT begins. The training/work/internship must either be REQUIRED for completion of your degree program (i.e., ALL STUDENTS IN THE PROGRAM MUST COMPLETE AN INTERNSHIP TO RECEIVE THE DEGREE) or you must be officially enrolled in an official internship or practicum course AND be receiving academic credit for the internship/practicum at the time of the training. NOTE: Failure to enroll in and complete the class will result in immediate violation of your legal status. It is the student’s responsibility to fulfill all requirements of CPT. There are restrictions on when students may apply for part or full-time CPT. Students can take CPT: Part-time (20 hours or less) or Full-time (more than 20 hours) : during the summer vacation or between semesters. Part-time : during the course of study provided the training does not exceed 20 hours per week total. Note : You cannot apply for CPT at all once you have completed your program of study. Students authorized for part-time CPT cannot work more than 20 hours per week. There is no limitation upon the length of time you may participate in full-time CPT, but if you participate for 12 months or more, you will not be eligible for optional practical training (see below) You cannot work off-campus under any circumstances until you have been authorized by the coordinator of international student services. IV. Other Important Information A. Curricular Practical Training and Eligibility for Optional Practical Training If you participate in 12 months or more of “full-time” CPT, you are not eligible to apply for optional practical training. However, if you participate in less than 12 months of full-time CPT, you will still get all 12 months of optional practical training. Participation in authorized “part-time” CPT does not “add up” and therefore, does not affect your eligibility for optional practical training. B. Employment Eligibility Verification When you begin work, you and your employer must complete a form entitled “Employment Eligibility Verification” (USCIS Form I-9), which the employer retains. The I-9 is provided by your employer and must be updated each time you receive a renewal of your work permission. This form requires you to document your identity and work authorization according to directions on the back of the form. The most convenient combinations of the various items acceptable as documentation include: your I-20 with the Curricular Practical Training work authorization, a valid passport, and an I-94 card marked for F-1 student status. Your employer, who keeps Form I-9, may make copies of the documents you submit, and return the originals to you. You will also need a Social Security card. If you do not already have a Social Security card, or if you have a card which is marked “not valid for employment” take your passport, I-94 Departure Record (can be obtained at https://i94.cbp.dhs.gov/ ), form I-20, and letter from the office of International Student Services to the office of Social Security Administration, and letter from your employer stating the beginning date of employment and apply for a new Social Security card. Note that your number will remain the same if you already had one, but the notation on the card should change to indicate that employment is valid with authorization. Contact the ISS Office for assistance. C. Social Security and Other Taxes In general, F-1 students who have been in the US less than five years are “non-residents for tax purposes” and are exempt from Social Security (FICA) and Medicare taxes (see Internal Revenue Service Publication 519, “U.S. Tax Guide for Aliens”). However, your earnings are subject to applicable federal, state, and local taxes. Tax returns must be filed on or before April 15 each year for the previous calendar year, which will determine if any of the withheld taxes can be refunded. V. text: CPT restrictions won’t bear positive results - Daily Trojan CPT restrictions won’t bear positive results Restricting international students will hurt the future of all American nationals. By PIRIL ZADIL September 4, 2026 (Piril Zadil / Daily Trojan) As I sat at my desk, about to begin my shiny new internship with Los Angeles magazine, I encountered unwelcome news: Curricular Practical Training, a form of institutionally awarded authorization that international students have used to work off-campus for the past 50 years, will no longer be available to most of us . This crackdown on CPT began with a letter sent by the United States Student and Exchange Visitor Program to all SEVP-certified U.S. universities Aug. 12. In it, SEVP requested stricter enforcement of CPT qualifications, limiting its use to students for whom “without [CPT], they would be unable to complete their degree.” Most University programs rarely mandate CPT; incredibly few of the over 100 undergraduate majors at USC actually require internships. Yet, in an industry climate where securing job offers without prior work experience is virtually impossible, it’s inaccurate to argue that CPT isn’t integral. By overlooking the value of CPT for international students, SEVP may have failed to consider the impact of losing students who won’t want to study in the U.S. without it. Daily headlines, sent straight to your inbox. Subscribe to our newsletter to keep up with the latest at and around USC. When I was a senior in high school applying to colleges, a factor I considered substantially was whether I could gain valuable fieldwork experience in the country I would choose to study in. This was especially important to me because my home country lacked the professional experience I sought; in another country, I could have the rare opportunity to pursue my dreams. My friends similarly chose their countries of study based on their future professional paths. The incoming class of international students, unable to pursue the opportunities we coveted, might be deterred from American colleges. International student enrollment has already declined in the past year, during which the Trump Administration has consistently made unpopular changes to nonimmigrant visas. The Association of International Educators estimated that international students’ economic contributions to the U.S. economy dropped by $1.1 billion from the 2023-24 to the 2024-25 academic year. The monumental economic downturn equated to the loss of 23,000 jobs for American nationals. On Aug. 11, before SEVP’s letter was even sent to universities, NAFSA estimated that the U.S. economy stood to lose $3.4 billion from the decrease in incoming international students. I imagine that, with CPT on top of it all, the loss will increase tremendously. With CPT off the table, international students who still want to pursue off-campus experience will gravitate toward other opportunities that do not require CPT approval. Some will lean toward volunteering with non-profit organizations, some will try to freelance from their home countries during the summer, but others won’t give up on U.S. work experience at all. One of the only remaining realistic ways for the latter to gain experience here is by applying for pre-completion Optional Practical Training. On the surface, CPT and pre-completion OPT are practically the same: Both allow a student to work while continuing their studies. But unlike CPT, which is processed by a Designated School Official, OPT is processed at the federal level by the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. As such, it requires a roughly $500 application fee. While these fees will initially contribute to USCIS’s operating revenue, the Department of Homeland Security has access to the organization’s funds. Notably, DHS has recently developed a habit of moving funds from USCIS and its other departments to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE. All in all, stricter enforcement of CPT regulations, which may seem like a minor change at first, will have a series of butterfly effects. International student enrollment will gradually decline, the U.S. gross domestic product will decrease, the economy will recede and American nationals will lose more jobs. Simultaneously, the government will grow richer. Is the U.S. government’s war against immigration truly worth the resources, dreams and hopes of American nationals? text: USG approves resolution supporting international students, curricular practical training - Daily Trojan USG approves resolution supporting international students, curricular practical training President Syrabi Nur Rahman announced she is working on free Canva Pro and LinkedIn Premium for students By DANIEL ESQUEDA October 28, 2026 Senator Piper Kujawa discussed her current projects, including an additional polling booth on USC’s campus and gathering data regarding student safety. (Adrian Jao / Daily Trojan) The Undergraduate Student Government approved a resolution Tuesday night in support of international students. Senate resolution 146-10, which passed unanimously, calls on the USC Office of International Services and the academic departments of each of USC’s schools to provide clear timelines for international students regarding when they can resume applying for curricular practical training. CPT is the federal work authorization that allows F-1 international students to complete paid or unpaid off-campus internships and practicums as part of their degree program. After students secure an internship offer at USC, they must register for an internship course before they can submit their CPT work authorization requests. Daily headlines, sent straight to your inbox. Subscribe to our newsletter to keep up with the latest at and around USC. On Aug. 24, a broadcast message was issued by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program, a program within United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement, stating that CPT requests for elective courses not required of every student in a program would no longer meet the requirements for approval for degree credit. “USG exists to serve every student, regardless of where they come from or what path brought them here,” said senator Leilani Akwue, who authored Tuesday’s resolution. “This includes our international students who contribute to this campus every day and deserve the same advocacy and support as everybody else.” Senators also unanimously approved senate bill 146-09 to amend USG’s funding department guidelines and allocations committee guidelines. Student organizations requesting funding must submit their travel expenses at least nine academic weeks before the initial payment due date, which includes transportation and hotels. Funding application deadlines have been extended for events taking place during the beginning of the Spring 2027 semester. Chief financial officer Jackson Alexander — who presented the bill — said the reason for the nine academic week deadline was to “clear up some confusion with the wording.” Alexander also said the funding application deadlines for spring semester events were extended to allow registered student organizations to have “a little bit more time” to get their applications in. Beyond these two items, senators unanimously approved SB 146-11 to recognize the statewide midterm election on Nov. 2 as a USG holiday and therefore cancel the senate meeting scheduled for that day. Speaker of the senate Madison Troup said the goal is to “allow and encourage” students, senators and USG members to vote. During reports of officers and directors, president Syrabi Nur Rahman announced that some of her completed projects include Zipcar discounts, tabling on Trousdale Parkway to connect with students, creating rest spaces at Leavey Library and expanding the RSO liaison position to four positions. “I think it is very important to let the student body hold us accountable for what we do, because our platform is our to-do list and our platform derives from knowing what USG can do and what USC needs as a campus,” Rahman said. “Part of our responsibility as your elected president and vice president is spearheading the undergraduate student government through these projects and through these initiatives that we promise to give you.” According to Rahman, projects that are in progress include obtaining free Canva Pro and LinkedIn Premium for students, town hall meetings, and a volunteer fair. In her presentation, vice president Diane Kim highlighted the 60 out of 128 projects that are now available to view on the USG legislative tracker. “We have 11 [projects] completed out of the 60 on the list,” Kim said. “The reason why it is 11 [projects] and not 60 is because a lot of these are long-term projects that will probably be getting done later throughout this year.” Additionally, chief of staff Shrinidhi Sriram said that throughout the month, she has been hosting bi-weekly organization-wide meetings, tracking office hours for all USG officers and coordinating stipends. One of Sriram’s projects included creating a how-to guidebook for USG officers. “[The how-to guide] is a passion project and a way for people to reference resources that we have available at USG,” Sriram said. “[The guide] serves as an accessible document where every USG officer can reference conduct, procedural expectations and any questions they might have.” Senator Piper Kujawa discussed her current projects, which include gathering data regarding how safe students feel on campus after students raised concerns about scooter safety, as well as an additional polling booth on USC’s campus in collaboration with VoteSC. “I reached out to the [Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk] office, and we are currently gathering data that is representing a gap in need and accessibility for civic engagement at USC because we have a lot of registered California voters,” Kujawa said. text: The Latest Change to International Student Policies: New Restrictions on CPT Authorization - Campus Times News The Latest Change to International Student Policies: New Restrictions on CPT Authorization Photo Staff By Yenah Park October 27, 2026 International students’ eligibility for internships, clinical experiences, and other forms of practical training has been restricted following a change in guidance from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) earlier this semester. The URochester International Services Office (ISO) announced that these new restrictions will affect international students with F-1 status who are waiting for approval for their Curricular Practical Training (CPT). According to an email from the University’s Office for Global Engagement, the SEVP’s new guidance has resulted in the following: 1. CPT authorization will now be granted only for practical training required for all students enrolled in a program to earn their degree. Internships and other experiential learning associated with elective courses or academic credit no longer qualify for CPT authorization. 2. The University’s Office for Global Engagement is carefully reviewing the new guidance and working with University leadership and academic programs to assess its implications for students and degree programs. 3. For the duration of this review, ISO is pausing approval of new CPT applications, except for requests associated with practical training required for completion of a degree program. 4. If a student’s CPT has already been approved for their Fall 2026 semester internships or training experiences, they may continue under the terms of that authorization unless ISO contacts them with different guidance. The email also emphasized that students should not begin off-campus employment or any activity requiring CPT authorization unless they have received approval from ISO. Sandra Pittenger, Assistant Director for Student and Scholar Advising Services at ISO, responded to students’ questions seeking clarification on the University’s stance towards the new guidance and the options currently available to international students at URochester. “The change to CPT stems from the government’s new interpretation of the term ‘integral to the curriculum,'” Pittenger said. “Previously, this was interpreted more broadly.” While only a handful of requests submitted to ISO were directly affected at the time of the initial authorization pause, Pittenger explained that the full extent of the changes may be difficult to quantify for the time being. “ISO is the final step in the CPT authorization process and does not make the initial eligibility determination,” Pittenger explained. “This is a widespread change, and even if someone was not directly impacted at the time of the initial pause, they may be impacted going forward.” Students who no longer qualify for CPT have a few potential alternatives. Pittenger identified pre-completion Optional Practical Training (OPT), another form of employment authorization for eligible F-1 students, as one option, though eligibility and timing may vary depending on individual circumstances. Pittenger confirmed that the regulations and guidelines governing pre-completion OPT remain unchanged. She also emphasized the importance of appointments, drop-in advising, and consultations with academic advisors and ISO as resources for students seeking to better understand their options. Looking ahead to Spring and Summer 2027, Pittenger recommended that students begin planning their internships early, determine whether practical training is required for their degrees, and consult ISO regarding employment authorization. “Federal immigration policies and guidance can change, so we can’t predict with complete certainty what requirements might be in place by next year or even next semester,” Pittenger said. “ISO will continue to monitor federal guidance and keep the University community updated on any changes as they happen.” Sophomore Ahmed Adhmed, Students’ Association Government (SA) senator and chair of the International Student Affairs Committee (ISAC), has also expressed plans to support international students through these changes. ISAC is currently encouraging students to share their concerns and feedback through a form posted on the SA Government’s Instagram page. Additionally, the committee hopes to “communicate more information for student-led organizations” representing “diverse and international backgrounds,” as well as share updates from ISO in future Campus Times articles.
